value.title: Bitcoin — Full Detail Knowledge Graph
value.description: Comprehensive machine-readable graph of Bitcoin's history, cryptographic primitives, UTXO transaction model, proof-of-work mining, consensus, Bitcoin Core C++ implementation context, wallets, scaling, privacy, economics, governance, and legal/ecological issues, based on the supplied article plus clearly labeled explanatory modeling.
value.source_basis: User-supplied Wikipedia article text with explanatory modeling and an explicit C-versus-C++ implementation clarification.

value.name: Peer-to-peer independent validation
value.description: Nodes relay data but independently apply consensus rules instead of trusting a central server.
benefits: No central ledger administrator
Independent verification
Resistance to accepting invalid state from a single service
tradeoffs: Bandwidth, storage, and validation costs
Network partitions can temporarily produce competing views

value.name: UTXO transaction lifecycle
value.description: Bitcoin value is represented as outputs created by prior transactions and consumed by later transactions.
flow: mark inputs spent and outputs unspent
benefits: Explicit ownership conditions
Straightforward double-spend checks against current UTXO state
tradeoffs: Coin selection affects privacy and fees
Change and fee handling require wallet logic

value.name: Proof-of-work block production
value.description: Miners assemble candidate blocks and repeatedly hash header variants until the result meets the target.
flow: vary nonce and other header data
benefits: Makes block creation resource-costly
Lets nodes verify a solution cheaply
tradeoffs: High electricity and hardware expenditure
Mining-pool concentration can weaken decentralization

value.name: Most-accumulated-work chain selection
value.description: Nodes choose among valid competing histories based on accumulated proof of work.
flow: switch to the valid most-work chain when needed
benefits: Deterministic fork-choice rule from node perspective
Older history becomes more expensive to replace as work accumulates
tradeoffs: Settlement confidence is probabilistic
Recent transactions can be reversed by sufficiently powerful competing work

value.name: Coinbase issuance and miner compensation
value.description: A valid block's coinbase transaction claims the scheduled subsidy and fees from included transactions.
flow: create coinbase claim within consensus limits
benefits: Rule-based issuance without a central issuer
Economic incentive to secure the chain
tradeoffs: Subsidy declines over time
Long-term security depends increasingly on fee revenue and other economic conditions

value.name: Wallet key custody and signing
value.description: Wallets manage key material, create transactions, and produce authorization proofs while the network validates them.
flow: receive outputs locked to a script
benefits: Users can self-custody without an account administrator
Offline signing can reduce key exposure
tradeoffs: Lost keys can mean unrecoverable funds
Exposed keys can enable theft; custodial services introduce counterparty risk

value.name: Base-layer and second-layer scaling
value.description: Base-layer block capacity constraints motivate systems such as Lightning that move many payment updates off-chain.
flow: settle channel state on-chain when needed
benefits: Can reduce base-layer transaction demand
Can improve payment latency and throughput
tradeoffs: Channel liquidity and routing constraints
Not every operation is free of base-layer dependencies

value.name: Pseudonymous public ledger and chain analysis
value.description: Addresses obscure identities at the protocol layer but transaction graphs remain public and can be analyzed.
flow: associate clusters with known identities where evidence permits
benefits: Public auditability and verifiability
tradeoffs: Address reuse and transaction patterns can reveal links
New addresses do not guarantee anonymity

value.name: Bitcoin Core C++ implementation architecture
value.description: The supplied article identifies Bitcoin Core as the open-source implementation written in C++. This is a conceptual mapping of major subsystems, not a claim that the project is written in C.
flow: wallet logic manages keys and transaction construction
benefits: Modular implementation of a distributed protocol
Open-source review and independent builds
tradeoffs: Large systems codebase with security-critical edge cases
C++ semantics and project APIs matter; illustrative C pseudocode is not drop-in Bitcoin Core code

value.name: Protocol upgrade and ecosystem coordination
value.description: Consensus and software upgrades require coordination among developers, miners, node operators, wallets, and businesses.
flow: participants choose whether and when to upgrade
nodes enforce their configured consensus rules
benefits: Changes can be developed transparently
Users and operators retain independent rule-enforcement choices
tradeoffs: Coordination can be slow and contentious
Incompatible rules can cause persistent forks

value.rule: A transaction input must reference an available unspent output and satisfy its spending conditions.
value.implication: A valid signature alone is not sufficient if the referenced output is missing or already spent.

value.rule: A node independently validates blocks against consensus rules.
value.implication: A miner's block is not accepted merely because the miner found proof of work.

value.rule: A Bitcoin proof-of-work block header must hash below the current target under double SHA-256.
value.implication: The target defines the acceptable hash threshold.

value.rule: The valid chain with the greatest accumulated work is preferred over a competing valid chain.
value.implication: Block count alone is an incomplete description of fork choice.

value.rule: Difficulty is recalculated every 2,016 blocks to target an average block interval near ten minutes.
value.implication: Actual block times vary; ten minutes is a long-run target, not a timer.

value.rule: A coinbase transaction may claim only the permitted subsidy plus eligible fees.
value.implication: Nodes reject blocks that create excess value even if the block has valid proof of work.

value.rule: The block subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks.
value.implication: Issuance declines over time and approaches a total below 21 million BTC.

value.rule: A bitcoin is divisible into 100,000,000 satoshis under the unit model described in the article.
value.implication: The satoshi is the smallest base unit in this model.

value.rule: Private keys must remain secret and backed up safely.
value.implication: Key exposure can enable theft; loss of all valid key material can make funds inaccessible.

value.rule: Bitcoin addresses and transaction histories are public, even though addresses do not directly state civil identities.
value.implication: Bitcoin is pseudonymous rather than inherently anonymous.

value.rule: Generating a new address can reduce some linkability but does not guarantee privacy.
value.implication: Public transaction patterns and external identity information can still connect activity.

value.rule: A majority-hash-rate attacker may reorganize recent blocks or censor transactions, but cannot force fully validating nodes to accept invalid transactions.
value.implication: Hash power does not override signature, supply, or block-validity rules.

value.rule: More confirmations generally increase the cost of reversing a transaction, but do not provide absolute mathematical finality.
value.implication: Risk tolerance and transaction value influence appropriate confirmation policy.

value.rule: Wallet software manages keys and transaction construction; bitcoin is represented on-chain as UTXOs, not stored inside the wallet application.
value.implication: A wallet backup protects key/recovery material rather than copying coins.

value.rule: The article identifies Bitcoin Core as written in C++, not C.
value.implication: C-like pseudocode can illustrate concepts but must not be mistaken for compilable Bitcoin Core source.

value.rule: A transaction's fee is the difference between its input value and output value, subject to valid transaction rules.
value.implication: A wallet must account for fee and change-output handling.

value.rule: Mining pools reduce individual payout variance but can aggregate decision-making and hash power.
value.implication: Pool concentration is a network-level risk even if many individual machines participate.

value.rule: A lightweight client does not provide the same independent full validation as a fully validating node.
value.implication: Convenience and lower resource use can entail reliance on peers or servers.

value.rule: Bitcoin's price is floating and has historically been volatile.
value.implication: Market price risk differs from the protocol's deterministic issuance schedule.

value.rule: Bitcoin's protocol-level fungibility does not prevent services from analyzing or discriminating based on transaction history.
value.implication: Technical interchangeability and market treatment are distinct properties.

value.rule: A soft fork tightens or changes rules in a way intended to remain compatible with non-upgraded nodes under defined conditions; a hard fork can be incompatible.
value.implication: Upgrade type influences coordination and chain-split risk.

value.rule: Lightning payment channels use off-chain state updates and depend on the base chain for relevant settlement operations.
value.implication: Second-layer payments reduce on-chain load but do not eliminate base-layer dependencies.

value.rule: A valid proof of work is easy to verify relative to the repeated computation required to find it.
value.implication: Nodes can cheaply check a candidate block's hash against the target.

value.rule: The 21-million figure is a rounded description; the article notes a theoretical total of 20,999,999.9769 BTC.
value.implication: Use exact-supply claims with the article's qualification.

value.rule: Legal status and compliance duties vary by jurisdiction and may change over time.
value.implication: Historical legal status should not be presented as current universal advice.

value.title: Alice pays Bob using a UTXO
value.scenario: Alice's wallet selects spendable outputs, creates an input referencing them, creates a payment output to Bob, optionally creates change, signs the spend, and broadcasts it.
steps: Wallet queries available UTXOs
Construct inputs and payment/change outputs
Calculate fee from input-output difference
Sign according to each input's script condition
Nodes validate and relay the transaction
A miner includes it in a valid block
caveats: The wallet does not contain the coins; the ledger tracks UTXOs.
A broadcast transaction is not yet confirmed.

value.title: Miner finds a block
value.scenario: A miner builds a candidate block and searches for a header hash below the current target.
steps: Select transactions from a mempool
Build a candidate block and coinbase transaction
Try nonce and other header variations
Double-hash the header with SHA-256
Check hash against target
Broadcast a successful candidate
Nodes independently validate it
caveats: Finding a valid hash is probabilistic and can require many attempts.
Other miners may find a competing block at nearly the same time.

value.title: Two blocks appear at once
value.scenario: Network latency leads different nodes to see competing valid blocks at the same height.
steps: Each branch is validated independently
Miners extend one or both branches
Nodes compare accumulated work
Nodes converge on the valid branch with more work
Transactions only in the losing branch may return to mempools if still valid
caveats: This is a normal possible network event, not automatically evidence of an attack.

value.title: Multisignature treasury
value.scenario: A script requires signatures from multiple distinct keys before funds can be spent.
steps: Create an output locked to a multisignature script
Distribute signing authority to separate key holders
Construct a transaction when spending is authorized
Collect required signatures
Nodes validate the script and input
caveats: Key loss and coordination failures can still prevent spending.

value.title: Cold-storage signing
value.scenario: A user keeps keys offline and transfers an unsigned or partially constructed transaction to an offline signer.
steps: Prepare transaction details on an online device
Review destination and amount on a trusted display
Sign with offline key material
Return signed transaction to an online device
Broadcast to the network
caveats: Offline custody reduces some remote risks but does not prevent all physical, supply-chain, or user-interface attacks.

value.title: Lightning payment
value.scenario: Two parties route a payment through payment channels rather than recording every update on the base chain.
steps: Open or use existing channel liquidity
Exchange off-chain channel updates
Route payment through channel network
Use the base chain for relevant channel settlement
caveats: Liquidity, routing, online availability, and channel management affect usability.

value.title: Public-ledger privacy risk
value.scenario: An address is not directly a person's name, but transaction patterns may link it to other addresses and known identities.
steps: Observe public transactions
Cluster addresses using spending patterns
Associate a cluster with an exchange or published identity
Infer links to other activity with varying confidence
caveats: Inference can be probabilistic and should not be treated as proof of identity without corroboration.

value.title: C-like educational model of a UTXO spend
value.scenario: Illustrative pseudocode models the logic of checking inputs and creating outputs. It is not production Bitcoin code and does not represent the full Bitcoin Script or consensus implementation.
value.code_language: C-like pseudocode (illustrative only; Bitcoin Core is C++)
caveats: Educational simplification only: omits integer-overflow-safe arithmetic, serialization, locktime/sequence rules, script execution details, witness handling, fee policy, consensus edge cases, and implementation APIs. Never use as a consensus implementation.
steps: Use a simplified UTXO lookup to reject missing or already-spent inputs
Check spending authorization for each input
Sum input and output values
Reject outputs exceeding inputs
Treat the result only as a conceptual sketch, not full consensus validation

value.title: Bitcoin — supplied Wikipedia article text
value.source_basis: The attached article text supplied by the user; its history, design, mining, wallets, scaling, economics, and regulatory sections inform this graph.
value.citation: The attached Bitcoin article begins with the article metadata and overview and continues through references and further reading.
limitations: Historical and time-sensitive figures are represented as claims reported by the supplied article, not independently verified current data.
This graph adds explanatory conceptual links and the C-versus-C++ clarification; those links are identified as explanatory modeling rather than verbatim article claims.

validation_notes: All relationship source and target IDs resolve to defined entities.
Entities and relationships are a conceptual knowledge graph, not a substitute for the Bitcoin consensus specification or source code.

fields.label: Notes
value: Primary source is the user-provided Bitcoin article text. Facts explicitly time-bound in that text (release version, circulating supply, price records, legal status, energy estimates, mining geography, and institutional holdings) must be read with their stated dates.

Implementation-language correction: the supplied article says Bitcoin Core is written in C++. C and C++ are related but distinct languages. The included C-like example is only educational pseudocode, not actual Bitcoin Core code.
Bitcoin is not a file or balance stored inside a wallet. On-chain value is tracked through UTXOs; wallets manage keys and transaction construction.
The 'longest chain' phrase is a shorthand. Consensus selection is more accurately described as the valid chain with the greatest accumulated proof of work.
Proof-of-work mining does not make invalid transactions valid. Fully validating nodes enforce consensus rules independently of miner hash power.
Bitcoin privacy is pseudonymity: the public transaction graph may support chain analysis, and new addresses do not guarantee anonymity.
Bitcoin's total issuance is commonly rounded to 21 million BTC; the supplied article gives a theoretical total of 20,999,999.9769 BTC.
Not investment, legal, tax, or cybersecurity advice. Laws, market conditions, and implementation details can change.

derived_rules.implication: Key exposure can enable theft; loss of all valid key material can make funds inaccessible.

derived_rules.rule: Bitcoin addresses and transaction histories are public, even though addresses do not directly state civil identities.
derived_rules.implication: Bitcoin is pseudonymous rather than inherently anonymous.

derived_rules.rule: Generating a new address can reduce some linkability but does not guarantee privacy.
derived_rules.implication: Public transaction patterns and external identity information can still connect activity.

derived_rules.rule: A majority-hash-rate attacker may reorganize recent blocks or censor transactions, but cannot force fully validating nodes to accept invalid transactions.
derived_rules.implication: Hash power does not override signature, supply, or block-validity rules.

derived_rules.rule: More confirmations generally increase the cost of reversing a transaction, but do not provide absolute mathematical finality.
derived_rules.implication: Risk tolerance and transaction value influence appropriate confirmation policy.

derived_rules.rule: Wallet software manages keys and transaction construction; bitcoin is represented on-chain as UTXOs, not stored inside the wallet application.
derived_rules.implication: A wallet backup protects key/recovery material rather than copying coins.

derived_rules.rule: The article identifies Bitcoin Core as written in C++, not C.
derived_rules.implication: C-like pseudocode can illustrate concepts but must not be mistaken for compilable Bitcoin Core source.

derived_rules.rule: A transaction's fee is the difference between its input value and output value, subject to valid transaction rules.
derived_rules.implication: A wallet must account for fee and change-output handling.

derived_rules.rule: Mining pools reduce individual payout variance but can aggregate decision-making and hash power.
derived_rules.implication: Pool concentration is a network-level risk even if many individual machines participate.

derived_rules.rule: A lightweight client does not provide the same independent full validation as a fully validating node.
derived_rules.implication: Convenience and lower resource use can entail reliance on peers or servers.

derived_rules.rule: Bitcoin's price is floating and has historically been volatile.
derived_rules.implication: Market price risk differs from the protocol's deterministic issuance schedule.

derived_rules.rule: Bitcoin's protocol-level fungibility does not prevent services from analyzing or discriminating based on transaction history.
derived_rules.implication: Technical interchangeability and market treatment are distinct properties.

derived_rules.rule: A soft fork tightens or changes rules in a way intended to remain compatible with non-upgraded nodes under defined conditions; a hard fork can be incompatible.
derived_rules.implication: Upgrade type influences coordination and chain-split risk.

derived_rules.rule: Lightning payment channels use off-chain state updates and depend on the base chain for relevant settlement operations.
derived_rules.implication: Second-layer payments reduce on-chain load but do not eliminate base-layer dependencies.

derived_rules.rule: A valid proof of work is easy to verify relative to the repeated computation required to find it.
derived_rules.implication: Nodes can cheaply check a candidate block's hash against the target.

derived_rules.rule: The 21-million figure is a rounded description; the article notes a theoretical total of 20,999,999.9769 BTC.
derived_rules.implication: Use exact-supply claims with the article's qualification.

derived_rules.rule: Legal status and compliance duties vary by jurisdiction and may change over time.
derived_rules.implication: Historical legal status should not be presented as current universal advice.

examples.title: Alice pays Bob using a UTXO
examples.scenario: Alice's wallet selects spendable outputs, creates an input referencing them, creates a payment output to Bob, optionally creates change, signs the spend, and broadcasts it.
steps: Wallet queries available UTXOs
Construct inputs and payment/change outputs
Calculate fee from input-output difference
Sign according to each input's script condition
Nodes validate and relay the transaction
A miner includes it in a valid block
caveats: The wallet does not contain the coins; the ledger tracks UTXOs.
A broadcast transaction is not yet confirmed.

examples.title: Miner finds a block
examples.scenario: A miner builds a candidate block and searches for a header hash below the current target.
steps: Select transactions from a mempool
Build a candidate block and coinbase transaction
Try nonce and other header variations
Double-hash the header with SHA-256
Check hash against target
Broadcast a successful candidate
Nodes independently validate it
caveats: Finding a valid hash is probabilistic and can require many attempts.
Other miners may find a competing block at nearly the same time.

examples.title: Two blocks appear at once
examples.scenario: Network latency leads different nodes to see competing valid blocks at the same height.
steps: Each branch is validated independently
Miners extend one or both branches
Nodes compare accumulated work
Nodes converge on the valid branch with more work
Transactions only in the losing branch may return to mempools if still valid
caveats: This is a normal possible network event, not automatically evidence of an attack.

examples.title: Multisignature treasury
examples.scenario: A script requires signatures from multiple distinct keys before funds can be spent.
steps: Create an output locked to a multisignature script
Distribute signing authority to separate key holders
Construct a transaction when spending is authorized
Collect required signatures
Nodes validate the script and input
caveats: Key loss and coordination failures can still prevent spending.

examples.title: Cold-storage signing
examples.scenario: A user keeps keys offline and transfers an unsigned or partially constructed transaction to an offline signer.
steps: Prepare transaction details on an online device
Review destination and amount on a trusted display
Sign with offline key material
Return signed transaction to an online device
Broadcast to the network
caveats: Offline custody reduces some remote risks but does not prevent all physical, supply-chain, or user-interface attacks.

examples.title: Lightning payment
examples.scenario: Two parties route a payment through payment channels rather than recording every update on the base chain.
steps: Open or use existing channel liquidity
Exchange off-chain channel updates
Route payment through channel network
Use the base chain for relevant channel settlement
caveats: Liquidity, routing, online availability, and channel management affect usability.

examples.title: Public-ledger privacy risk
examples.scenario: An address is not directly a person's name, but transaction patterns may link it to other addresses and known identities.
steps: Observe public transactions
Cluster addresses using spending patterns
Associate a cluster with an exchange or published identity
Infer links to other activity with varying confidence
caveats: Inference can be probabilistic and should not be treated as proof of identity without corroboration.

examples.title: C-like educational model of a UTXO spend
examples.scenario: Illustrative pseudocode models the logic of checking inputs and creating outputs. It is not production Bitcoin code and does not represent the full Bitcoin Script or consensus implementation.
examples.code_language: C-like pseudocode (illustrative only; Bitcoin Core is C++)
caveats: Educational simplification only: omits integer-overflow-safe arithmetic, serialization, locktime/sequence rules, script execution details, witness handling, fee policy, consensus edge cases, and implementation APIs. Never use as a consensus implementation.
steps: Use a simplified UTXO lookup to reject missing or already-spent inputs
Check spending authorization for each input
Sum input and output values
Reject outputs exceeding inputs
Treat the result only as a conceptual sketch, not full consensus validation

notes: Primary source is the user-provided Bitcoin article text. Facts explicitly time-bound in that text (release version, circulating supply, price records, legal status, energy estimates, mining geography, and institutional holdings) must be read with their stated dates.

Implementation-language correction: the supplied article says Bitcoin Core is written in C++. C and C++ are related but distinct languages. The included C-like example is only educational pseudocode, not actual Bitcoin Core code.
Bitcoin is not a file or balance stored inside a wallet. On-chain value is tracked through UTXOs; wallets manage keys and transaction construction.
The 'longest chain' phrase is a shorthand. Consensus selection is more accurately described as the valid chain with the greatest accumulated proof of work.
Proof-of-work mining does not make invalid transactions valid. Fully validating nodes enforce consensus rules independently of miner hash power.
Bitcoin privacy is pseudonymity: the public transaction graph may support chain analysis, and new addresses do not guarantee anonymity.
Bitcoin's total issuance is commonly rounded to 21 million BTC; the supplied article gives a theoretical total of 20,999,999.9769 BTC.
Not investment, legal, tax, or cybersecurity advice. Laws, market conditions, and implementation details can change.

value.name: Publish content and join a BitTorrent swarm
value.summary: A publisher creates torrent metadata, publishes a .torrent file or magnet link, seeds the complete content, and clients discover peers and exchange verified pieces.

steps.action: Prepare the files and choose piece length and metadata parameters.
Generate torrent metadata and piece hashes; v1 uses SHA-1 and v2 uses SHA-256/Merkle-tree structures.
Publish the .torrent file or magnet link through an index or another distribution channel.
Make a complete copy available so initial downloaders can obtain pieces.
Discover peers through trackers, DHT, and/or peer exchange.
Exchange pieces with peers; verify received pieces against metadata hashes.
Reassemble verified pieces into the file and optionally continue seeding.

value.name: Peer discovery with tracker, DHT, and PEX
value.summary: Peer discovery can combine centralized trackers, decentralized DHT lookup, and peer exchange. These mechanisms are complementary rather than mutually exclusive.

steps.action: Read tracker endpoints from torrent metadata when present.
Ask tracker services for peers, if reachable.
Join the DHT via a bootstrap server and look up peers when DHT is enabled.
Exchange peer information with connected peers using PEX when supported.
Connect to candidate peers and repeat discovery as peer membership changes.

value.name: BitTorrent v2 integrity verification and hybrid compatibility
value.summary: BitTorrent v2 uses SHA-256 and Merkle-tree-based hashes for finer-grained integrity checks. Hybrid metadata includes v1 and v2 hashes to support older and newer clients.

steps.action: Hash content at file and piece granularity using the v2 format.
Obtain the torrent metadata or equivalent magnet metadata.
Transfer pieces from one or more peers or web seeds.
Verify the received content against the expected hash tree.
For hybrid torrents, use the included v1/v2 metadata to interoperate with compatible legacy and v2 clients.

value.name: Piece selection and reciprocal uploading
value.summary: A client selects available pieces, prioritizes rare pieces to preserve diversity, and uses choking/unchoking policies plus optimistic unchoking to manage upload partners.

steps.action: Track missing pieces and the pieces advertised by connected peers.
Prefer rare pieces to reduce the chance that a piece disappears from the swarm.
Use choking/unchoking decisions to allocate upload bandwidth.
Use optimistic unchoking to try a peer that may become a better exchange partner and help newcomers acquire initial pieces.
Verify and share successfully received pieces, increasing swarm capacity.

value.name: Hybrid peer and web-seed distribution
value.summary: A publisher can combine conventional HTTP/FTP hosting with peer-to-peer delivery, using the web server as an initial or fallback source while the swarm takes on increasing load.

steps.action: Host the content on a web server and publish torrent metadata.
Obtain pieces from the web seed and from peers where available.
Upload received pieces to other peers.
Optionally reduce or stop direct web serving when the swarm has enough seeders.

value.name: BitTorrent privacy and trust boundaries
value.summary: The base protocol exposes peer IP addresses and does not provide anonymity. VPNs, seedboxes, Tor-like systems, or I2P change the trust and visibility model but introduce their own constraints.

steps.action: Connect to swarm peers; peer endpoints may be visible to other participants.
If using a VPN or seedbox, recognize that the intermediary can observe some user activity or network metadata.
If using Tor-like routing, consider client compatibility and network impact; the article cautions that most clients are not designed for safe torrenting over Tor.
Treat downloaded payloads as untrusted and verify integrity; a valid hash proves correspondence to metadata, not that the content is benign or legally authorized.

value.name: Swarm availability failure and recovery
value.summary: A swarm can lose availability when all complete seeds disappear. Multiple discovery paths do not solve missing-content availability; durable seeds, bundling, or cross-torrent strategies can help.

steps.action: Download pieces and optionally seed them after completion.
Remain online to provide a complete source for missing pieces.
If no complete seed remains and required pieces are missing, the download may stall indefinitely.
Improve long-term availability by maintaining seeds, bundling related content, or using proposed cross-torrent cooperation.

value.core_mechanism: Content is divided into pieces. Clients discover peers using trackers, DHT, and/or PEX; exchange pieces across many connections; verify pieces using hashes; reassemble files; and can continue uploading pieces to other peers.
key_architecture_tradeoffs: Distribution capacity can grow as peers join, but a swarm still needs sufficient seeders and piece availability.
Trackers are straightforward but add a centralized discovery dependency; DHT and PEX provide alternative discovery paths.
Rarest-first improves piece diversity, while non-sequential downloading can complicate streaming playback.
v2 improves hashing and granular integrity verification; hybrid torrents preserve compatibility with v1-only clients.
The base protocol does not provide anonymity; privacy overlays change who can observe network endpoints and add trust or performance tradeoffs.
Cryptographic integrity does not establish that content is benign or legally authorized.
important_distinctions: Torrent metadata and indexes are discovery artifacts; the payload is transferred between peers.
A tracker coordinates peer discovery; it is not ordinarily the source of the file bytes.
A seed has the complete content; a downloading peer may have only some pieces.
DHT peer discovery does not itself guarantee that any peer still has the missing pieces.
Protocol legality is distinct from whether a particular distribution is authorized.
Historical traffic and malware statistics in the article should not be interpreted as current universal measurements.
